title: Learning From Mistakes Versus Learning From Explanations
author: Andrew Watson
summary: Andrew Watson summarizes a 2024 British Journal of Educational Psychology study by Janet Metcalfe, Robert Bjork, and colleagues that compared explicit re-teaching to error-focused review for four teachers helping 175 eighth-graders prepare for a high-stakes math exam. Both review approaches improved scores, but the learn-from-mistakes group improved more on average, and the size of that advantage varied dramatically by teacher -- from 2% to 5% gain per hour of instruction. The study's authors ruled out overall teacher quality and time spent addressing errors as explanations, since both variables were similar across the most and least successful teachers. The real difference came down to two variables: whether the teacher focused on correct procedure versus the nature of the error, and whether the interaction was lecture or discussion. The most successful teacher spent almost all her time in discussion, evenly split between solving problems and understanding mistakes, while the least successful teacher lectured about correct procedure. Watson is careful to note the finding is scoped to review sessions with motivated volunteer students, not initial instruction, and closes by arguing the field should stop litigating labels like 'desirable difficulty' versus 'productive struggle' and instead ask whether students are both thinking harder and ultimately succeeding.
points: The study isolated two variables -- teacher focus (procedure vs. nature of the error) and interaction style (lecture vs. discussion) -- as the actual drivers of the learn-from-mistakes advantage, after ruling out overall teacher quality and time-on-errors as explanations.
The most successful teacher divided her discussion time evenly between solving problems correctly and understanding why errors occurred, rather than favoring one over the other.

The finding is explicitly scoped to review sessions with already-taught, motivated students preparing for an exam -- not a general claim that mistake-driven learning beats direct instruction during initial teaching.

Watson's closing point reframes the desirable-difficulty-vs-productive-struggle debate as largely semantic: the operative question is whether students are thinking harder and ultimately succeeding, not which label applies.
quotes: In this study, 4 teachers helped 175 8th grade students prepare for upcoming state math exams.
The students in the “learn-from-mistakes” group learned more.
The least successful teacher helped students in this group improve 2% per hour of instruction. The most successful teacher helped students improve 5% per hour of instruction.
As the researchers write: “all of the teachers taught to the errors of their students, and … the extent to which they did so did not predict student learning.
Teacher M — whose students improved more quickly — spent almost all her time in discussion, with almost no time in lecture.
This study does NOT argue that "learning from mistakes" is better than "direct instruction" in all circumstances.
My own view is: don't get hung up on the label. The question is: are the students both thinking harder and ultimately succeeding?
